title: Slopes and local change
outcome: By the end, I can explain slopes and local change using a traced example and a stated limitation.
scenario: Use a local slope to propose a small move rather than claiming every move helps.
given: Toy loss J(a)=(a-2)². At a = 0, use symmetric step 0.5.
All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

steps.label: Check small move
steps.detail: Move to a = 0.25: loss 3.0625, below starting loss 4.

explanation: A slope describes how the loss changes near the current parameter. The symmetric calculation compares equal small moves on either side. Its negative result suggests a small increase may help at zero. It does not promise every increase helps: jumping to five passes the optimum at two and produces a larger loss. Check the new loss after each proposed step.

counterfactual.change: Move from 0 all the way to5.
counterfactual.reason: A negative local slope suggests increasing a locally, not that every positive jump decreases loss.

student_task: Which calculation disproves “any increase helps”? Point to the relevant step in the picture, then write the changed result and the rule or evidence that supports it.
teacher_answer: J(5)=(5-2)²=9>J(0)=4. The local direction is useful only with an appropriately sized step and verification. Changed-case check: Loss becomes9, exceeding the starting4. A negative local slope suggests increasing a locally, not that every positive jump decreases loss.
project_evidence: For your Image-pattern Network Investigation, save the input, procedure, observed result and limitation of this check. Label this worked example as practice; use a different, previously unreviewed case when checking independent understanding.
limits: A finite difference approximates local change; numerical precision and nonsmooth points need care in more complex objectives.
